newsitem.title: USA: Intel says inventory lower than it wants.
newsitem.headline: Intel says inventory lower than it wants.

text.p: Intel Corp's Pentium and Pentium Pro microprocessors are selling so rapidly that the chip maker is having trouble keeping inventory at a comfortable level, a top executive said.
With its factories working at full capacity, Intel ended December with $1.293 billion of inventory in its pipeline.
"This is less than we would like to have," said chief financial officer Andy Bryant in a conference call. "We will increase it when the opportunity arises."

During the fourth quarter, when Intel's sales shot up to $6.4 billion, its inventory level fell about $80 million, Bryant said. The company's aim is to restore at least that much to its pile of work in progress this quarter, he said.

But Bryant said inventories held by distributors and manufacturers who put its products in personal computers and other devices seem to be in good shape. Intel supplies microprocessors for 90 percent of the PCs sold worldwide. It expects the market to grow at a "high teens" percentage yearly on average over five years, Paul Otellini, executive vice president and director of worldwide sales and marketing said.
The worldwide PC market has grown at such rates in the past several years, he added.
Intel has typically helped fuel sales by lowering the prices of its microprocessors about four times a year. Its next round of price cuts is planned for February 1, the executives said.
To be sure, Intel skipped a price cut in November, and sales were still much stronger than Wall Street analysts had expected.
Bryant and Otellini said fourth-quarter sales got a big boost from corporations upgrading their personal computers.
Corporations typically buy personal computers equipped with its Pentium Pro microprocessors, they said.

Intel will introduce an upgraded version of the Pentium Pro, called the Klamath, in the second quarter, the analysts said. The new chip will incorporate Intel's so-called MMX, or multimedia extensions technology, which enhances a personal computer's video, graphics and audio presentations. Intel introduced an MMX version of its Pentium chip this month.
Otellini also said Intel would introduce a version of its P6 or Pentium Pro chip notebook computers this year.

Intel, with about 90 percent of the market, would appear to have little competition. But Advanced Micro Devices Inc plans to introduce a chip with many of Klamath's features during the first quarter --- ahead of Intel.
Analysts said Advanced Micro told them that major PC manufacturers were sampling its K6 entry.
Intel, responding to an analyst's question on how the K6 might affect its marketing plans for the Klamath, said Advanced Micro's chip was having no influence on its discussions with PC makers.
